title: Detection Strategy for AutoHotKey & AutoIT Abuse
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for AutoHotKey & AutoIT Abuse
summary: This strategy detects abuse of the AutoHotkey and AutoIt scripting environments (T1059.010), which are legitimate Windows automation tools that adversaries frequently reuse because they are signed, widely present and easy to weaponise. Compiled scripts appear as ordinary executables, and scripting hosts can automate keystrokes, read window content and load external code, so detection cannot rely on file names alone. The strategy correlates process creation with command lines, script file writes, module loads of the automation runtime and outbound network activity from the same process. It fails when the organisation legitimately uses automation scripts for testing or accessibility, because then the parent process, script location and signing status are the only fields that separate work from abuse.

beginner.definition: This detection watches two popular Windows automation tools. These tools can press keys and click buttons for a user. Attackers use them because they are normal, signed programs. The detection looks at how the tools are used, not just that they exist.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers prefer tools that already exist on the machine. Such tools raise fewer questions and often pass allow lists. These automation programs can also mimic a real user, which fools activity checks. Watching their behaviour gives you a signal where a simple file rule would stay silent.
howItWorks: The computer records the program start, the account and the full command line.
The detection looks for the automation hosts and for compiled scripts built from them.
It notes where the script file lives, because a downloads or temporary folder is unusual for business tooling.
It checks the parent program, since a mail client or a web browser is not a normal parent for automation.
It looks for extra clues such as the runtime loading from a strange folder or the process making a network connection.
The event is scored, and anything outside the approved tooling pattern is sent to an analyst.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse with a forklift. Forklifts are allowed and useful, so nobody questions one. But a forklift driven out of the loading bay at night is different. The driver has no shift record and carries a crate to a waiting van. That is worth a second look. The vehicle was never the problem; the use of it was.
takeaways: Popular signed tools can become attacker tools, so behaviour beats block lists.
The script path and the parent program are your best clues.
Keep a record of approved automation so unusual parents and paths stand out.

objectives: Explain why legitimate automation tools attract attackers
Identify process, file and module telemetry that reveals automation tool abuse
Judge script file locations and parent processes against an approved baseline
Spot compiled automation scripts that hide their source
Draft a rule that stays useful without blocking a legitimate automation workflow
dataSources: Windows Security event 4688 process creation with command line auditing enabled
Sysmon event 1 process creation including parent image, current directory and full command line
Sysmon event 11 file create events for script files written to user, download or temporary directories
Sysmon event 7 image load events showing the automation runtime loaded by a process
Sysmon event 3 network connection made by the automation host to an external address
logic: The pattern is an automation host or a compiled automation script running from a user-writable, download or temporary location, started by a parent that is not a build service or a test runner, and often followed by a network connection or by window manipulation of other applications. The fields to correlate are the process image, the command line and any script path argument, the parent image, the directory the process runs from, the loaded automation runtime and the signing status of the image. The benign case is a test engineer running a signed automation script from a source repository folder, with a developer tool as parent, during working hours. The malicious case is an unsigned compiled script in a temporary folder, a parent such as an office document or a web browser, and an outbound connection to an address unrelated to the build pipeline.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Automation Script Host Executing From User Writable Path
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection:
#     EventID: 1
#     Image|endswith: ['\\AutoHotkey.exe', '\\AutoHotkeyU64.exe', '\\AutoIt3.exe', '\\SciTE.exe']
#   filter_approved:
#     ParentImage|endswith: ['\\devenv.exe', '\\code.exe', '\\jenkins-agent.exe']
#     Image|startswith: 'C:\\Program Files\\AutoIt3'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: Quality assurance teams that run signed automation scripts to drive application user interface tests
Accessibility tools that use automation scripting to remap keys for users with motor difficulties
IT staff who deploy small automation scripts from a network share to standardise desktop tasks
Business users running locally written scripts that move data between approved desktop applications
Packaging engineers who compile automation scripts as part of a normal release build
tuningNotes: Enumerate every approved automation use case, capture the parent process, install path and code signing identity, and filter only that combination so a new script location still alerts. Alert on execution from download, temporary and user profile directories at full severity, since approved workflows rarely use them. Add a companion rule for unsigned compiled scripts that load the automation runtime, which catches the case where the host is renamed. The coverage you lose by allow listing your known automation paths is a script placed there by an attacker with write access, so pair this rule with file integrity monitoring of approved script directories.
